finding.claim: delete_file discards the result of is_allowed, so any caller, including one with no identity, can delete any file in STORE.
finding.source: Any request to DELETE /files/<fid>; g.user is None when the X-Session-User-Verified header is absent (views.py:12).
finding.sink: del STORE[fid] at views.py:19, a protected destructive operation.

trace.note: require_allowed(g.user, f, 'delete') is called; its bool return value is discarded.
require_allowed is an alias for is_allowed, a pure predicate that returns a bool and never aborts.

finding.guards_checked: before_request (views.py:10-12) only sets g.user and enforces nothing. acl.is_allowed (acl.py:4-5) returns a bool and does not raise. acl.ensure_allowed (acl.py:8-10), which would abort(403), is not used on this route. No decorator or middleware guards the route.

verdict.guard_found: none effective. views.py:18 calls require_allowed, which is acl.py:4 is_allowed, a bool-returning predicate that never aborts. Its result is discarded as a bare statement, so views.py:19 runs unconditionally. ensure_allowed (acl.py:8-10, abort(403)) is imported at views.py:3 but used only on the rename route (views.py:26). before_request (views.py:10-12) only sets g.user and enforces nothing.
verdict.reason: The DELETE handler at views.py:18 discards the bool from require_allowed (alias of is_allowed, acl.py:4-5), which never raises, so views.py:19 deletes the file for any caller, including one with no X-Session-User-Verified header (views.py:12 sets g.user to None), and no other control intervenes. The trace is accurate, and the attacker needs only anonymous network access and a valid fid.

finding.claim: The acting identity is read from a client-supplied header with no verification, so a caller can impersonate any user when the app is reachable without a trusted proxy that sets and strips the header.
finding.source: HTTP header X-Session-User-Verified, fully attacker-controlled on direct access.
finding.sink: Authorization identity used in acl.is_allowed grants lookup (acl.py:5), reached via ensure_allowed in rename_file (views.py:26) and is_allowed in delete_file (views.py:18).

trace.note: ensure_allowed evaluates is_allowed for the header-supplied user.
The grants lookup is keyed on the attacker-supplied user, so an attacker can claim any user that holds write or delete grants.

finding.guards_checked: No check in this code verifies that the header originated from a trusted upstream, and no code strips it from external requests. The header name suggests a proxy sets it, but that is not enforced here. Exploitability depends on deployment, which I could not verify.

verdict.guard_found: none. views.py:12 takes the header with no verification, and no code strips or validates it. acl.py:9-10 (ensure_allowed) is an effective abort(403) guard, but it only checks whatever identity the header supplies. The bare require_allowed(...) call at views.py:18 discards its bool, so delete_file has no effective check at all.
verdict.reason: views.py:12 trusts the client-supplied X-Session-User-Verified header as the caller's identity, and acl.py:5 and acl.py:9-10 then authorize on that value, so a direct caller can claim any user with write grants and rename files (views.py:26). The claim's dependence on a trusted proxy is a deployment fact the code cannot verify, but the code itself has no check. Separately, views.py:18 is a bare call to is_allowed whose result is discarded, so DELETE /files/<fid> is unauthorized for every caller, which is a stronger issue than the one the candidate described.
